 The Real Cost of Trump’s ‘Big Beautiful Bill’ Is Just Beginning
 PUBLISHED 11/9/2026 by 
 Gaylynn Burroughs , Amy Matsui and Kathryn Menefee 
 Many of the law’s most consequential cuts to healthcare, food assistance and education were deliberately delayed until after the 2026 midterm elections, leaving millions of Americans bracing for the worst.
 Volunteers with africActive pack boxes at a free food distribution at Rancho Cienega Park on Aug. 29, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. Major cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) under President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act are expected to leave an estimated 650,000 Californians at risk of losing food assistance, prompting food banks to prepare for increased demand as more people seek help with groceries. (Justin Sullivan / Getty Images) 
 This article originally appears in the Fall 2026 issue of Ms ., as “The Bill That Keeps on Taking.” Become a Ms . member today and get print issues delivered right to your mailbox. 
 In July 2025, Republicans in Congress passed, and President Donald Trump signed, this administration’s signature piece of legislation: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). The massive law was enacted under special rules that make it easier to pass legislation without bipartisan engagement or support. In addition to directing unprecedented levels of funding toward the administration’s anti-immigrant detention and deportation agenda, the OBBBA slashed funding for programs that help people afford food, healthcare and education to pay for trillions of dollars in tax cuts that overwhelmingly benefit the wealthiest people and corporations.
 Its supporters claimed that the law would allow Americans to “keep more money in their pockets,” but for families trying to make ends meet, the reverse is true. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates that households in the lowest 10 percent of income distribution will lose about $1,600 per year over nine years, amounting to nearly 4 percent of their income. And the law is already raising costs on groceries, healthcare and education for women, men and children across the country who benefit from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the Affordable Care Act, Medicaid and federal student loans.
 But the worst is yet to come. The OBBBA was specifically designed to delay many of its harmful measures until after the November 2026 midterm elections.
 The Damage Has Begun
 Even though accessing affordable healthcare has often ranked as a top concern for U.S. workers, the OBBBA will strip millions of women and their families of lifesaving healthcare services through its steep cuts to Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (more than a trillion dollars in less than a decade); the expiration of credits designed to help families afford health insurance premiums; and a one-year “defunding” of Planned Parenthood and some independent abortion providers. Researchers estimate that more than 5 million people lost health coverage in the year following the law’s enactment. And the OBBBA isn’t even fully implemented.
 In anticipation of a massive loss of federal Medicaid dollars, lawmakers in several states are already entertaining cuts to critical care services for vulnerable families, including to home- and community-based services for people with disabilities and older adults. These cuts would be especially devastating to care workers—made up almost entirely of women, primarily Black women and Latinas—who often rely on Medicaid for their healthcare and for their wages.
 In 2023, Medicaid covered about one-fifth of all hospital spending, and upon discharge, 1 in 5 patients relied on Medicaid to pay for their hospital care. Since the law passed, more than 1,000 hospitals, clinics and nursing homes have shut down or cut services, or are at risk of doing so due to anticipatory cuts, including in rural and underserved areas.
 The OBBBA also allowed the enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits to expire at the end of 2025. The loss of these credits, which helped families with low incomes afford health insurance, has made the cost of insurance premiums rise sharply for many enrollees—by an average of 58 percent per month—causing millions of people to forgo health insurance altogether. The CBO estimates that by 2034, the expiration of these credits will prevent 4.2 million people from becoming insured.
 Finally, the legislation blocked patients from using Medicaid to receive care at Planned Parenthood for one year, though thanks to court challenges, that period ended up being slightly shorter. Patients who rely on Medicaid made up around half of all visits to Planned Parenthood before the “defunding” took effect in September 2025. A year later, nearly 30 Planned Parenthood health centers have been forced to close, leaving thousands of people without access to essential healthcare, including cancer screening, STI testing and contraception. A recent analysis from the National Partnership for Women & Families found that these closures, along with other pre-OBBBA closures in 2025, have had the greatest impact on women of color, especially Latinas.
 In addition to stripping women and families of healthcare, the OBBBA is also causing families to go hungry. The law slashed federal spending for SNAP (formerly the food stamp program) by an estimated $187 billion—a fifth of the program’s total funding—over the next nine years. 
 As part of these cuts, the OBBBA ended benefits for many lawful immigrants and expanded SNAP’s ineffective work reporting requirements, newly applying them to adults ages 55 to 64 and caregivers for children ages 14 and older, and removing exemptions for veterans, youths who have aged out of foster care and people experiencing homelessness. Most SNAP recipients who can work do. A research review conducted by the Brookings Institution revealed that SNAP’s work reporting requirements do not increase employment; instead, they create barriers that prevent eligible people from accessing needed food assistance.
 Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks during a press conference at the Javits Center on July 1, 2026, in New York City to mark the one-year anniversary of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. (Michael M. Santiago / Getty Images) 
 The law’s restrictions on SNAP eligibility are already having devastating consequences for millions of families. According to an analysis of U.S. Agriculture Department data by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, from July 2025, when the OBBBA was enacted, to April 2026, SNAP participation nationwide fell by more than 4.5 million people.
 The OBBBA has already changed the way SNAP benefits are calculated, preventing them from keeping pace with food prices and nutrition standards and blocking any real reevaluation until 2027. This means that for the roughly 42 million people who rely on SNAP—the majority of whom are women, and about 1 in 3 of whom are women of color—benefits will fall further behind food price inflation each year. Even before the OBBBA, the maximum SNAP benefit fell short of monthly meal costs by $53, according to the Urban Institute.
 The reduction in SNAP benefits will wreak havoc on the lives of women and their children. As one home care worker and mother of two tells Ms. , “I already struggle to balance the rising costs of rent, utilities, transportation, groceries and other necessities. SNAP helps me put food on the table when my paycheck is not enough to cover everything. Without SNAP, I would have to make impossible choices between buying groceries, paying rent, keeping the lights on or meeting my children’s needs.”
 Meanwhile, the legislation is cutting off pathways for economic opportunity for lower-income individuals, including access to higher education. The OBBBA creates new student loan limits and provides fewer repayment and forgiveness options for the Parents PLUS Loan program for parents of undergraduates, meaning that more students may have to rely on expensive private loans to finance their education, or forgo higher education altogether.
 And as first proposed by the Heritage Foundation in 2024, in July of this year the OBBBA eliminated the Grad PLUS Loan program, which allowed students to access federal loans to borrow up to the full cost of attendance (minus any financial aid received) in a graduate program. It also capped annual and lifetime student loan borrowing for new borrowers, the majority of whom are women.
 “These policies do not alleviate the student debt crisis or make postsecondary education more accessible or affordable,” says Ashley Harrington, senior policy counsel at the NAACP’s Legal Defense Fund.
 One estimate finds that the average Grad PLUS borrower who replaces their loan with a private market option will pay an additional $10,855 in interest—if they can secure financing at all. These restrictions especially impact women, who disproportionately take out more loans than men, and threaten to compound the already harmful economic effects of the gender pay gap. The heaviest burden will fall on Black women, who are less likely than any other group to receive loan-repayment help from family and friends and who rely on loans at disproportionately high rates.
 Furthermore, the new lifetime borrowing limits are stricter for graduate degrees designated by the Department of Education as “non-professional,” including dental hygiene, social work, teaching and public health. These degrees, according to National Women’s Law Center calculations, are primarily held by women. Students who hold these degrees go on to perform essential work as healthcare professionals, educators and public servants.
 Curtailing these opportunities will directly affect all of our communities, while negatively impacting educational institutions that serve women, low-income borrowers and Black students, including historically Black colleges and universities. Harrington says the changes under the OBBBA “will critically diminish Black students’ ability to access higher education.”
 Delayed by Design
 Republican leaders and the Trump administration made sure that many of the OBBBA’s most harmful measures would not go into effect until after the November 2026 midterm elections.
 A banner with a portrait of U.S. President Donald Trump is displayed on the front U.S. Department of Labor Frances Perkins Building on May 30, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter / Getty Images) 
 The most significant impacts from the Medicaid cuts are still to come, for one. Beginning in January, people ages 19 to 64 who are enrolled in Medicaid through the Affordable Care Act’s expansion will be required to report at least 80 hours per month of work (or other activities that qualify, including school) to access or maintain Medicaid coverage. The law does not fully exempt people with caregiving responsibilities from these work reporting requirements, which will especially harm women. Medicaid expansion enrollees will also have their eligibility for the program checked every six months, instead of every year as under prior law. 
 Taken together, 5 million to 10 million people could lose Medicaid coverage in 2028.
 Also in 2028, states will have to implement cost-sharing for the Medicaid expansion population. Under the law, participants will have to pay up to $35 per healthcare service. Cost-sharing increases financial burdens on families, causes worse health outcomes and deters many people from pursuing needed healthcare. One study found that even cost-sharing of as little as $1 to $5 prevented some individuals with low incomes from pursuing needed care. And cost-sharing disproportionately hurts women, who are both more likely to have low incomes and more likely to have chronic conditions.
 The CBO estimates that all the OBBBA changes to health programs will lead to about 10 million people losing their coverage by 2034. These coverage losses will be especially devastating for women, who represent the majority of individuals enrolled in Medicaid. 
 As Heather Thomas, an American parent, explains, “Without Medicaid our family would not have insurance. It is a lifeline.”
 In addition to these looming coverage losses, upcoming SNAP changes will shift more costs to the states, causing many more people to lose access to food assistance. Under prior law, the federal government covered the full cost of SNAP benefits and evenly split administrative costs with the states. However, the OBBBA will force states to take on 75 percent of the administrative costs in October of this year and will require them to pay a share of the food benefits starting in October 2027. Most states will have to pay double or triple the amount that they spend today on SNAP, and the costs will be especially high for states with above-average poverty rates.
 Ultimately, though, much of these costs will fall on families. Many states cannot afford the millions, if not billions, of dollars it would take to cover the law’s cuts. Because many states are required to balance their budgets annually, they will either need to raise additional revenues or reduce benefits and services—including, but not limited to, nutrition assistance and healthcare.
 And some states are making the “perfect storm” caused by the OBBBA even worse. 
 North Carolina state Sen. Sophia Chitlik (D) explains that in her state, even as they are receiving less money from the federal government, the Republican-controlled state legislature is moving to cut both income and corporate taxes and preempt the ability of counties to levy property taxes. In her view, this poses an “existential threat” to SNAP and Medicaid, as well as other social services programs, and counties are going to be bearing the brunt. 
 When combined with the impacts of the Trump administration’s other economic policies and funding cuts, she says, “We’re going to see nonprofits and philanthropy continually being asked to do government’s job.”
 There are also more harms on the horizon for student loan borrowers. New borrowers are already required to be on more expensive repayment plans as of July. One estimate finds that a typical new borrower with a bachelor’s degree will pay more than $4,000 per year under the new repayment assistance plan. And starting in July 2028, millions of loan borrowers who are on pre-OBBBA plans will be forced to move to the new, more expensive repayment plans, which could increase their student loan costs by more than $3,400 per year.
 Small Perks, Big Costs
 Even as millions of people have lost healthcare, food assistance and support for higher education—and millions more will in the years to come—proponents of the OBBBA have portrayed some provisions of the law as beneficial for working families, such as the expansion of the child tax credit, child savings accounts (otherwise known as Trump Accounts) and the “no tax on tips” provision.
 While the OBBBA increases the child tax credit by $200 per eligible child for families making up to $400,000 per year, the law leaves in place an existing exclusion that denies the full credit to roughly 17 million children whose families’ incomes are too low to qualify, including roughly 45 percent of Black children and 60 percent of children in families headed by single mothers. And the law prevents millions more previously eligible families from benefiting from the child tax credit at all—including 2 million children from immigrant families, most of whom are citizens and lawful permanent residents, but will be denied unless both parents have a Social Security number. 
 Overall, for families in the bottom 20 percent of the income distribution, the OBBBA decreased the average benefit by about $100.
 The newly created Trump Accounts also overwhelmingly benefit wealthier families. While the federal government will seed eligible accounts with one-time $1,000 contributions for babies born between 2025 and 2028, any further contributions to the accounts must come from families, employers or philanthropists. Many lower- and middle-income families simply will not be able to afford to make additional contributions, and employer contributions are voluntary, meaning these accounts will likely become de facto tax shelters for higher-income households.
 Similarly, the “no tax on tips” provision provides little to no benefit for most workers. This provision eliminates federal income taxes on the first $25,000 of tip income for workers paid less than $150,000 per year. But more than one-third of tipped workers have earnings so low that they were already exempted from income tax. Overall, the Tax Policy Center estimates that only 3 percent of households will benefit from the provision in 2026.
 More generally, preliminary data from the 2026 tax filing season suggests that the tax benefits for those of us who aren’t billionaires were largely overblown: Average refunds increased by around 11 percent, which is less than the $1,000-$2,000 increase per household that administration officials were promising.
 The Price We’ll Keep Paying
 The law’s tax cuts for corporations and the wealthiest Americans and its funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement come with an astronomical price tag. The OBBBA will add more than $4 trillion to the federal debt over the next nine years, even with the historic cuts to SNAP, Medicaid and assistance for higher education. That means long-term ripple effects for everyone.
 First, the ballooning federal debt puts pressure on interest rates, making mortgages and credit card debt even more expensive. 
 Second, this budgetary black hole will likely be used as an excuse for why our government can’t fully fund federal programs and services that benefit us all. 
 And third, undoing the OBBBA’s cuts will require revenues commensurate with those lost under the law; more will be needed to make the investments women and families need to thrive, not just survive.
 The slow-rolling disaster unleashed by the OBBBA is unfolding amid the larger context of this administration’s agenda. Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran have caused the cost of food and other necessities, including housing, utilities, gas and transportation, to soar. The administration’s persecution of immigrants has exacted an extraordinary human toll, as well as an economic one. The so-called Department of Government Efficiency froze federal funds that millions of people in every state rely on, and slashed the federal workforce in agencies that help ensure families receive childcare services and Social Security benefits, protect students from discrimination at school, and more.
 In his second term, the president has pardoned three billionaires convicted of money laundering, insider trading and campaign violations, forgoing $141.4 million in restitution that would otherwise go to victims, with a portion headed into federal coffers.
 Meanwhile, the administration’s attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion and “gender ideology” have pushed women and people of color out of jobs, threatened workforce training programs and imperiled access to lifesaving services for survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault.
 Even as families’ budgets are squeezed, personal savings dwindle and credit card and other consumer debt rises, the incomes and wealth of billionaires continue to soar to unprecedented levels. And it’s no wonder: In May, the president openly admitted he wasn’t weighing ordinary families’ financial security “even a little bit” in his talks with Iran.
 The OBBBA’s disastrous and ongoing impacts are not happening in a vacuum. Women and people of color, who are already at higher risk of poverty and economic insecurity because of discrimination and systemic inequities, are struggling to afford skyrocketing costs as their earnings are not increasing at the same rate. Concern about the cost of living and the ability to afford healthcare, food and groceries remains high.
 Fall 2026 issue of Ms . (Photo by Jenny Warburg) 
 We may not see the full economic impacts of the second Trump administration for decades, between the delayed implementation dates of OBBBA cuts, the trickle-down effects in states, and the elimination of government data that would document health disparities, food insecurity and more.
 At the same time, here’s one thing we know from 250 years of the American experiment: Women are always going to find a way to take care of their families and communities.
 As Amalia Luxardo, CEO of the Women’s Rights and Empowerment Network, a South Carolina-based nonprofit, puts it: 
 “The story of women has never been one of waiting to be rescued. Across South Carolina, women are showing up for one another every day sharing resources, organizing neighbors, caring for families and refusing to let harmful policies define what’s possible. Laws can create barriers, but they cannot erase our power to build community. We know that when women are connected, informed and supported, they will continue to find ways not just to endure, but to lead lasting change.”
